newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania Senate passes bill on state bank selloff.
newsitem.headline: Romania Senate passes bill on state bank selloff.

text.p: The upper house of Romania's parliament, the Senate, approved on Monday a bank privatisation bill, a key demand under the reform package agreed with international lenders for renewed credits.
"The approval of the draft means a confidence vote for the (centrist) government," said Varujan Vosganian, president of the Senate's budget and finance commission.
The long-awaited bill, submitted to parliament last week and debated in emergency procedures, is to be discussed by the lower Chamber of Deputies next week.
Former bank selloff bills, benchmarks under previous loan accords with the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, failed to clear parliament twice in 1996.

Under the new draft, Romanian state-run banks will turn private by raising capital through share issues or by sales of stocks held by the majority shareholder, the State Ownership Fund (FPS), or through a combination of the two.
The FPS is allowed to retain a "golden share" in any bank going private, giving it the right to veto to such decisions as mortgages on assets, mergers or liquidation.
The selloff will be open to local and foreign individuals and corporate investors, who will pay cash for acquired stock.
Last week, Reform Minister Ulm Spineanu said Banca Romana pentru Dezvoltare development bank would be the first of six state-run banks to go private when the bill became effective.

An agency would be appointed to work out privatisation methods and set the maximum stake which can be acquired by investors and the type of shares to be issued. All these elements are subject to government's approval.
Senators amended an article saying returns from selloffs would become state budget revenues. They agreed the destination of returns would be set under a different law.

No single stockholder can acquire more than 20 percent of the equity, with the exception of reputed financial and banking institutions. Nor can purchases be made on the strengths of credits from local banks. Any share acquisition larger than five percent must be approved by the central bank (BNR).
The banking industry, including 40 commercial banks, is one of the fastest growing sector in post-communist Romania.

But, in recent years, the country's fledgling financial markets have been hit by scandals at two private banks, which now await court rulings on their liquidation or reorganisation. The BNR said it would soon withdraw their banking licences.
